text:
From that day on, nothing more had been heard of him. Though Marguerite had dismissed her guests and changed her habits, the duke had sent no further word. What I had gained from this was that my mistress belonged to me more completely, and that my dream was at last coming true. Marguerite could no longer do without me. Without troubling herself about what might result from it, she openly displayed our liaison, and I had reached the point of never leaving her house. The servants called me Monsieur and officially regarded me as their master.

Prudence had strongly remonstrated with Marguerite about this new life; but Marguerite had replied that she loved me, that she could not live without me, and that, whatever might come of it, she would not renounce the happiness of having me constantly beside her, adding that all those whom it displeased were free not to return.

That was what I had heard one day when Prudence had told Marguerite that she had something very important to tell her, and I had listened at the door of the room in which they had shut themselves.

Some time later Prudence returned.

I was at the far end of the garden when she entered; she did not see me. From the way Marguerite had come forward to meet her, I suspected that a conversation like the one I had already overheard was about to take place again, and I wanted to hear it as I had the other.

The two women shut themselves in a boudoir, and I began to listen.

“Well?” Marguerite asked.

“Well! I saw the duke.”

“What did he say to you?”

“That he readily forgave you for the first scene, but that he had learned that you were living openly with Monsieur Armand Duval, and that he did not forgive you for that. ‘Let Marguerite leave this young man,’ he told me, ‘and, as in the past, I shall give her whatever she wants; otherwise, she must give up asking me for anything whatsoever.’”

“What did you answer?”

“That I would convey his decision to you, and I promised him that I would make you see reason. Consider, my dear child, the position you are losing, a position Armand will never be able to restore to you. He loves you with all his soul, but he does not have enough fortune to provide for all your needs, and one day you will inevitably have to part, when it is too late and the duke is no longer willing to do anything for you. Do you want me to speak to Armand?”

Marguerite seemed to be reflecting, for she did not answer. My heart was beating violently as I waited for her reply.

“No,” she resumed, “I shall not leave Armand, and I shall not hide the fact that I live with him. It may be madness, but I love him! What can you expect? And besides, by now he has grown accustomed to loving me without hindrance; he would suffer too much if he were forced to leave me, even for just one hour a day. Besides, I have not so much time left to live that I should make myself unhappy and do the bidding of an old man whose very sight makes me grow old. Let him keep his money; I shall do without it.”

“But how will you manage?”

“I do not know.”

Prudence was no doubt about to answer something, but I burst in and ran to throw myself at Marguerite’s feet, covering her hands with the tears that my joy at being loved in this way made me shed.

“My life is yours, Marguerite; you no longer need that man. Am I not here? Would I ever abandon you, and could I ever repay sufficiently the happiness you give me? No more constraint, my Marguerite; we love each other! What does the rest matter to us?”

“Oh! Yes, I love you, my Armand!” she murmured, winding both arms around my neck. “I love you as I would not have believed I could love. We shall be happy, we shall live quietly, and I shall bid an eternal farewell to this life of which I am now ashamed. You will never reproach me for the past, will you?”

Tears veiled my voice. I could answer only by pressing Marguerite to my heart.

“Come,” she said, turning back toward Prudence and speaking in an emotional voice, “you will report this scene to the duke, and you will add that we do not need him.”

From that day on, there was no more talk of the duke. Marguerite was no longer the woman I had known. She avoided everything that might have reminded me of the life amid which I had met her. No wife, no sister, ever had for her husband or brother the love and care that she had for me. That sickly nature was open to every impression, receptive to every feeling. She had broken with her friends as she had with her habits, with her manner of speaking as she had with her former expenditures. When people saw us leave the house to go for a ride in a charming little boat I had bought, they would never have believed that this woman, dressed in a white gown, wearing a large straw hat and carrying on her arm the simple silk cloak that was to protect her from the coolness of the water, was that same Marguerite Gautier who, four months earlier, had caused a stir with her luxury and her scandals.

Alas! We hastened to be happy, as though we had guessed that we could not be so for long.

For two months we had not even gone to Paris. No one had come to see us except Prudence and that Julie Duprat of whom I have told you, and to whom Marguerite was later to entrust the touching account I have here.

I spent whole days at my mistress’s feet. We opened the windows overlooking the garden, and, as we watched summer descend joyfully among the flowers it brings into bloom and beneath the shade of the trees, we breathed side by side that true life which neither Marguerite nor I had understood until then.

This woman displayed a child’s wonder at the slightest things. There were days when she ran through the garden like a ten-year-old girl, chasing a butterfly or a dragonfly. This courtesan, who had caused more money to be spent on bouquets than would be needed to keep an entire family living in happiness, would sometimes sit on the lawn for an hour to examine the simple flower whose name she bore.

It was during that time that she read Manon Lescaut so often. Many times I caught her making notes in that book, and she always told me that when a woman loves, she cannot do what Manon did.

Two or three times the duke wrote to her. She recognized the handwriting and gave me the letters without reading them.

Sometimes the words of those letters brought tears to my eyes.
